The way I see it, welfare (defined in this case as collecting any type of
government money while not being gainfully employed) should be like a job.
When the government is helping someone get through the time between losing
one job and finding another, that person's JOB should be to FIND a job.

As I understand it (from someone who recently went through it), welfare
recipients are required to show evidence that they have talked with at least
two potential employers about employment every 2 weeks (to be honest, I
can't remember whether it's 1 week, 2 weeks, or 1 month, but I'm pretty sure
it wasn't every week). In my estimation, this is ludicrously low (even if
it was every week)! When I have been looking for a job, I must have sent out
no fewer than 6 resumes any given week (and that's even in a slow week) -- and
I still HAD a full time job!

See, the way I see it, they should have to be able to show that they spent
20+ hours per week (and that's treating it as a part-time job) looking for
work. In fact, as much as we spend in taxes to support the various welfare
programs, there ought to be a place where they can go to research jobs,
work on resumes, and even make phone call inquiries on jobs. If they aren't
able to show this (like with a list of companies and contact name/numbers
which could be randomly spot verified or by showing that they were at the
kind of center I just suggested we ought to have), or show that there was a good
reason why not (i.e. death or illness in the family), they could lose their
benefits (maybe they get one warning or something, but you get the idea).

Furthermore (as if I haven't been controversial enough yet), I think that
just like they could be with any regular employment, they should be subject to
random drug testing. If they fail, they get help or they lose their benefits
(and there ARE PLENTY of free or pay-as-you-are-able -- i.e. free for these
individuals -- drug programs available to those who want them).

Well that's my $.02 worth for now. I just thought I'd see what anyone thought
about my ideas and see if anyone else had other ideas to throw on the table.
I figure if enough ideas get thrown out there, something good (certainly better
than I see now) is likely to come out of it. The latest reforms are a good
start, but only time will tell how they play out. Of course, the biggest
problem with the latest reforms is that the govt. really doesn't have the
networked infrastructure to actually enforce them from one state to another,
but perhaps they'll figure out a way to fix that soon enough...

Jennifer

P.S. -- I know that some of you will abhor my ideas. If you do, please try
to attack the ideas, rather than the writer, and show why they are not viable.
That makes for a much more interesting discussion, in my opinion.


----------------------------------------------------------
My opinions are not necessarily representative of my employers'.

> jmi...@austin.ibm.com () wrote:
> >
> >The way I see it, welfare (defined in this case as collecting any type of
> >government money while not being gainfully employed) should be like a job.

> >When the government is helping someone get through the time between losing
> >one job and finding another, that person's JOB should be to FIND a job.

Seems to me there are three catagories of welfare recipients:

A) Capable of working, temporarily on welfare due to bad luck or local
economic conditions.

B) Capable of working, but scamming the system. Can't be too bright as
welfare doesn't exactly pay big bucks.

C) Incapable of holding a job in modern society because they are simply
dumb as dirt.

The original liberal welfare concept assumed that most recipients were in
catagory C (although nobody will come out and say that). The most cost
effective way of keeping these folks from starving to death was to just
send them a check. Setting up government infrastructure to help them
spend twenty hours a week sending out resumes would be like pissing our
tax dollars down the drain. The conservative welfare reformers are trying
to get everyone to believe that most welfare recipients are in catagories
A and B.

In fact, for a welfare reform plan to work, it must be flexible enough to
cost effectively deal with people in all three catagories. It must
actually help those in catagory A find jobs. It must identify and remove
from the system those in catagory B. And it must sustain those in
catagory C without trying to force them through training and job search
programs at which they will fail.

Dave

> "Too late to drown in all my doubt, too much too late to sort things out"--GK

Two things... first, Jeff, you mentioned a "strategy" -- do you have something
specific in mind? As I said in my original post, I'd like to hear others'
proposals on the subject as well.

Second, perhaps it's the eternal optimist in me, but I just don't see that
there is anyone, excluding people with real mental or physical (or both)
handicaps (who are a different story altogether), who is truly so dumb as to be
incapable of ANY work in this world. Sure, they may not be able to learn to
use a computer. Sure, they may not even be together enough to be able to work
at a fast food restaurant flipping burgers or cleaning tables. But surely they
could handle SOMETHING!

Maybe I just don't know anyone who is "dumb as dirt". On the other hand, I
do know people who have fallen somewhere between category A and B of Dave's
analysis and I do really believe that there are more people in those two
categories than in the third. I'm not seeking to "throw all the bums out."
I want to set an expectation of welfare recipients that discourages those who
can work, but just want to take a break for a while since they can, from
thinking of welfare as a way to take that break. People live up to the
expectations set for them. If you set your expectations too low, most people
will do what it takes to meet your expectations and nothing more. It's easy to
fall into a trap of laziness if people don't expect more than that from you.
(If you don't believe that, just look at the average high school student...
but that's another topic...)

Jennifer

At the heart of all history, in the clarity of our collective dream,
there are a few common themes. Among these there is a sword, and a
stone.

A sword is a terrible thing, an instrument of power, yet a magical
thing, a surgeon's healing blade imbued with light. A stone is a dark
and seemingly inert mass, a land or people.

In order to wield the sword of light, one must become one in the stone.

Movement without effort, action without exertion, this is the principle
upon which creation turns, as when, in spring the sun returns, in its
inexorable round revolving, brimming life in the simplicity and power
that elemental things have, animating the green fusion force that drives
the flower and splits the rock ...

I stood alone in a field at nightfall, remembering my history, caught
between earth and a clear winter sky. A host of stars arose from the
trees like birds and I thought, summoning fire from quickening life,
this is my life, our life, the place of our life.


from "Our Common Prayer"

jim sanders

I think we need to have a strategy, arrived at via due process of
course. I have some ideas, but I don't know if it could be considered
a "strategy". Some of these ideas are:

- Letting public welfare exist primarily at the state/local level
because those programs are more responsive and closer to the
community, with perhaps loose guidelines only at the federal level

- Setting the level of benefits to be less than minimum wage (but not
substantially so), so that there is a financial incentive to move out
of welfare

- Setting a time limit of some sort on welfare benefits, so that there
is a temporal incentive to move out of welfare

- Allowing subsidized (_not_ free) childcare for those who do get off
welfare, maybe even run by other welfare recipients

- Make it standard operational procedure to refer all new welfare
cases to private charities first -- that is, government welfare should
only be used as a last resort

- Require all welfare recipients either to be actively seeking a job
or to go to a job retraining class

- Set up a database in each community of those "in the system", among
private and public charities, to help make sure people don't fall
through the cracks but also to cut down on fraud

Just a couple of ideas off the top of my head.

Those who are "deserving" are the ones who legitimately are incapable of taking

> - Setting a time limit of some sort on welfare benefits, so that there

In primitive governments, people organized in order to provide
everyone with equal protection against violence and robbery.
As technology improved, governments could afford to give more
and more to their people, from public use of roads, to parks,
to libraries, sewage systems, even the right to receive mail.

Someday, technology will allow us to provide everyone with
shelter and food indefinitely. If it ever gets to the point
where we can easily produce 5 homes for everyone on the planet,
there's no reason not to give it to people only on moral grounds
that it will make them lazy. If welfare gave everyone $20K
a year, and I had the chance to make another $10K on top of
that just for doing an extra push-up everyday, you don't think
I'd do it? It's when people see little hope of bettering
their situation that they stop trying.

("The Crab's Credo" was originally posted on June 13, 1996)

The Moral Philosopher expounded on his characteristic mendacity:

>When will the Right Wing learn that it's this very aggressive
>intolerance that has turned the public against them and their leaders
>and has fried all hope of their remaining in power? The "angry white
>male" credo has turned their commentary into that of the "crabby Right

The "Right Wing" can answer for themselves.

I would point out that the "aggressi[on]" has been
undertaken unilaterally by the Warfare State against individual human
beings which it presumes to "serve"...whether individuals value its
"service" or not. There is no resort to reason which is available to
the grasp of this state's proponants. When the victims identify the
essential coercive nature of the state, and protest, they are met with
every sort of argument from "social contract"...a signed copy of which
has never been produced. Of course, the "social contract" is merely a
metaphor whose principles are easily exploded with diligent attention
to the details.

Nonetheless, the metaphor has become a handy device for
conscripting the lives of individuals to the service of this state.
It has "progressed" all the more so as the metaphor has passed from
cutting edge philosophy, to politics, to energetic public policy, to
ingrained habit and un-challenged metaphysical assumption.

There are people in this country today, Left and Right, who
do not know that a living must be earned, and that no one is
"entitled" to it.

They strut this violation of nature as analog to the divine
right of kings: the state as omnipotent in service of "society",
instead of the crown in service to God.

"It is well settled," we are told in the manner of an adult
dealing with a child asking a pertinent question, but who is too tired
to offer authentic reasons. Well, it is not "well settled", and the
hidebound, threadbare, political paternalism which has driven our
elders to poverty and wasted their years, will not do.

And, if reason won't do, then "eternal hostility" will be
the only recourse. "Reason" in this case, does not include
"negotiation". It will not abide any but the most rigorous
understandings of First Things: those essentials of identity which set
men apart from animals, able to choose their own values amid the
security of liberty to act to win them.

Any person willing to examine, in good faith, those
principles which brought a new political light to a dark world in the
American Revolution, is welcome to every possible expression of my
goodwill.

All others, Left or Right, are subject to my earnest,
passionate, emphatic, consistent, and lifelong, contempt.

To instant hell with them.

My outrage will be expressed solely on my own discretion.

THE PREMISE

Votescam asserts the unthinkable.

and mine may now be a meaningless bit of energy directed by preprogrammed
computers-which can be fixed to select certain pre-ordained candidates and
leave no footprints or paper trail.

In short, computers are covertly stealing your vote.


For almost three decades the American vote has been subject to
government-sponsored electronic theft.
The vote has been stolen from you by a cartel of federal "national
security" bureaucrats, who include higher-ups in the Central Intelligence
Agency, political party leaders, Congressmen, co-opted journalists-and the
owners and managers-of the major Establishment news media, who have
decided in concert that how America's votes are counted, by whom they are
counted and how the results are verified and delivered to the public is,
as one of them put it, "Not a proper area of inquiry."
By means of an unofficial private corporation named News Election
Service (NES), the Establishment press has actual physical control of the
counting and dissemination of the vote, and it refuses to let the public
know how it is done.


This book also contends that the theft of your vote or Votescam, is part
of a supposedly "patriotic collaboration" between federal officials and
the news media that began shortly after the assassination of John F.
Kennedy in 1963, when the "responsible" American press was persuaded by
American intelligence services to hide from the American people the actual
implications of the Kennedy murder. My brothers, Jim and Ken Collier,

snapping at their journalistic heels.

I, too, am a journalist and editor by profession, and a skeptic by
training. Yet, as hard as I have tried not to, I now believe they were
actually holding the tail of an elephantine conspiracy that they uncovered
inch by heart-rending inch.

After reading Votescam, the impatient citizen may well ask: "Why, if there
is truth in the charges, are there no indictments?"

That question is one of many provoked by Votescam's reporting, and if
Americans actually value their vote then there will be indictments based
on this book's data and documentation.

My brothers peeked behind Oz's curtain and into a voting booth where
people of power had secret hold of all the levers-as well as all the keys
on the computer keyboard.

Yes, that's one hell of a conspiracy and it-as Jim and Ken uncorked
it-doesn't stop there. You may be shocked, annoyed, angry, astounded or
alarmed to find out where and how deep my brothers feel it penetrates.

Votescam is one of the weirdest trips 1990s Americans may take. My hope is
that you will suspend disbelief for a while and read it with an open mind.
If it raises questions you will demand answers.

Answers to "improper inquiries" is what this book is about. It's what

Barnard L. Collier, New York City, 1992

Electronic Hoodwink


"We can now speak the most Majestic words a democracy can offer: 'The
people have spoken' .. "

-First words spoken by President-elect, George Bush, November 8, 1988

"Once, during the time when days were darkest I made a promise. Thanks,

Same speech, final words.


It was not "the People" of the United States of America who did "the
speaking" on that election day, although most of them believed it was, and
still believe so.

In fact, the People did not speak at all, and George Bush may have known
it or, at least, strongly suspected it.

The voices most of us really heard that day were the voices of computers -
strong, loud, authoritative, unquestioned in their electronic finality.
The computers counted more than 55 million American votes in 1988 - more
than enough to swing election after election across the nation. In that
election, a difference of just 535,000 or so votes would have put Dukakis
into the White House.

The computers that spoke in November 1988 held in their inner workings
small boxes that contained secret codes that only the sellers of the
computers could read. The programs, or Source codes," were regarded as
"trade secrets." The sellers of the vote-counting software zealously
guarded their programs from the public, from election officials, from
everyone on the dubious grounds that competitors could steal their ideas
if the source codes were open to inspection.

You may ask: What "ideas" does it require to count something as simple as
ballots?

Can the "ideas" be much more complex than, let's say, a supermarket
computerized cash register or an automatic bank teller machine?

The computer voting machines do not have to do anything complicated at
all; they simply must be able to register votes for the correct candidate
or party or proposal, tabulate them, count them up, and deliver
arithmetically correct additions. People with no formal training, even
children, used to do it all the time...

"The United States government has no elections office and does not attempt
to administer congressional elections. The responsibility for the
administration of elections and certification of winners in the United
States national election rests with a consortium of private entities,

formal structure of election administration in the United States is not
capable of providing the major TV networks with timely results of the
presidential and congressional elections. In the case of counting actual
ballots on national election night, public officials have abdicated
responsibility of aggregation of election night vote totals to a private
organization, News Election Service of New York (NES). NES is a

CBS and NBC and the press wire-services AP and UPI. __This private

arisen in the nation's press because the responsibility NES now has in
counting the nation's votes was assumed gradually over a lengthy period
without ever being evaluated as an item on the public agenda.__

This privately owned vote counting cartel (NES) uses the vast membership
of the network-subsidized League of Women Voters as field personnel whose
exclusive job is to phone in unofficial vote totals to NES on election
night. NES also operates a "master computer" in New York City, located on

volunteerism and do-goodism, the fact that it is actually a political club
with a political agenda and a hungry treasury is shrouded by the false
myth that it is a reliable election-day watchdog.)

The NES mainframe computer has the capability, via telephone lines, of
"talking" back and forth with county and state government mainframes.
During the important 60-day certification period after an election, the
counts in the county and state mainframes can still be manipulated by

Without this capability of using the NES mainframe to "balance the books "
between initial network projections of Bush as "winner" and the final
official totals published two months later, Bush may have lost the
election to Dukakis.

It is the prescription for the covert stealing of America.

I can't believe, in this day and age, that anyone can be ignorant that
for most of human history government did not exist. In most societies
government has recently been imposed.--I refer to so-called primitives.

Anarchism_. Furthermore, there have been the individualist-anarchist
communities founded by Josiah Warren--see Martin's _Men Against the
State_. Also, the Ukraine and Kronstadt movements, which were crushed
pretty quickly but it worked until that happened: see Arshinov and
Voline. I don't have a reference handy for the Spanish anarchists.
There are also many forms of social organization in our own society that
have no hierarchical structure--the internet, for one; for another, many
self-help groups (I exclude the AA's "higher power" shit from this
example).

I suspect the problem here is that some people confuse hierarchy with
organization. Anarchy is the opposite of hierarchy, is the form of
organization that emerges spontaneously when individuals act
voluntarily. Chaos, this is now called!--Complex order, self-ordering
rather than by control.

Anyway, do your homework before you make statements about whether
anarchy is possible or not. You have to go out of your way to find out
about the history of anarchy--don't rely on your handy ignorance.

Andrew Hall wrote:
> >>>>> Milt writes:

> Milt> ... But seriously, devaluation generally causes
> Milt> DEflation, not INflation, if it has any effect domestically...

> You have this backwards. Anything we had to buy
> from overseas gets more expensive in dollar terms
> if the dollar is devalued. But since we do not
> buy everything overseas Mr. Schneider's estimates
> are off.

Well, you have to look at time scales and other things that are
going on. Initially, a considerable devaluation has an
inflationary effect, the extent of which depends on percentage
of imports (and substitutability of goods that are imported).
However, it also stimulates the economy, because exporters have
a greater competitive advantage; thus, it improves balance of
payments, because imports decrease while exports increase. This
can lead to a reduction of interest rates, which always helps...
Depending on how much spare capacity there is in the economy,
there can be inflation (if the economy is working hard), or not
(if it isn't). In the latter case, there can be a virtuous
spiral as people come off the dole queues, reducing government
expenditures on welfare and increasing tax revenues. [A classic
example of this is the UK after the (unintentional) devaluation
a few years ago, which is why I can comment on it.]

Of course, the increasing strength of the economy tends to lead
to a higher exchange rate, so unless structural changes are
introduced during the transition, the only obvious response is
to devalue again, and then again, as the economy becomes
increasingly uncompetitive (again following the UK example).
Margaret Thatcher thought she understood the fundamental
UK malaise, and so tried to introduce the structural changes
she thought would result in subsequent success; unfortunately,
she didn't really understand the problem, so her "answer" didn't
help (hence the need for the devaluation of a few years ago).

Right you are, Frank. The TV license is about $140 this year (for
color; b&w is a little less. I guess if you can afford a color TV you
can afford more tax.) It's a yearly fee and is a site license only.

I have 'one low price' access to the internet but the local phone call
gets expensive @ 2 pounds per hour (somewhere over $3.00).

Most families I know here have only one car. There are lots of BMWs,
Mercedes, etc., and plenty or Rolls', but somewhere between 25% and
35% of the cars in use are ten years old or older. Many old people
just plain can't afford cars at all. They use the buses, cycle, or
walk. In this respect lack of autos is a plus. People are healthier.
Also, communities are more closely knit as people actually pass each
other on the sidewalks and stop to talk.

Some other differences I thought of since yesterday:

Many of the smaller businesses don't have any heat. Installing the
systems is a real expense in all the older buildings. How many
American workers would happily spend the day at work wearing gloves,
hat, and scarf? The wife and I both spend our days on computers
wearing gloves with the fingers cut out.

McDonalds is one of the few smaller businesses that have air
conditioning in the summer. I have yet to see a home with air.

Americans love the cute village markets they see when they visit, but
those vendors are ekeing out a meager living in all kinds of weather
year in and year out. It isn't that they were offered a nice big mall
space to rent and they turned their noses up at it, but that a square
of canvas and a rickety table and a pile of second hand merchandise to
hawk is all they can afford. And the natives that shop there are
patrons not because they're taken with the quaintness but because they
can't afford to go to Marks & Spencer or to Harrods or even to
Sainsburys or Safeway.


Anyway, I think I'm through on this thread, when do we pull Hillary's
fingernails out?

Another right-winger who has no idea what socialism is. If you had attempted this
explanation in an Econ 101 class, the professor would have thunked you over the head
with Paul Samuelson's introductory text "Economics" -- and it weighs three pounds.

Socialism means that workers, not private owners, would own and control the
means of production: factories, farmland, machinery, and so on. In democratic
elections, workers would vote for 1) their supervisors, 2) their representatives
to a local and national council of their industry or service, and 3) their
representatives to a central congress representing all the industries and
services. Socialism has been proposed in many forms, ranging from republics
to direct democracies, from centralized state bureaucracies to free market
anarchy. Political scientists do not view the "socialism" nominally practiced
by the Soviet Union as true socialism -- this was, essentially, a dictatorship
over workers by a ruling elite. In other words, socialism has never been tried,
let alone suffered a "100 percent record of failure."

By comparison, liberals believe that private owners should own and control the
means of production, formulate company policy, and have the right to select
their own management team. Liberals would prevent them from abusing their powers
through checks and balances like strong labor unions and democratic government.

If you can't even define the most basic terms of the debate correctly, you have
nothing to say about political or economic theory that I want to hear. Get thee
to a college class!

>There are several European nations that have a higher standard of living than
>ours. About half of them tend to socialism and half at least approach our
>level of free enterprise and relatively low taxes. I don't see a trend.

What are these countries with a "higher standard of living"? How was
this measured?

There are countries in EC with a higher compensation, I believe.
Germany is one, but there is more than simply compensation involved in
standard of living.

The first question you need to ask is if the compensation has been
adjusted for Parity Purchasing Power (PPP), which compensates for the
wide variety of prices found in different countries. For example,
here are some comparitive prices:

Germany US France Japan
steak 0.27 0.21 0.42 1.14
broiler 0.05 0.04 0.14 0.09
eggs 0.05 0.05 0.14 0.05
rice 0.11 0.05 0.18 0.09

(see US Statistical Abstracts, 1995, table 1379). Thus, if an egg
cost 27 cents in Germany, it is 21 cents in the US and so on.

There is also considerably more goods and services to go around. The
US has a considerable lead on the EC in GDP:

France $17,089
Germany 18,709
US 24,302
Japan 20,523
UK 17,036

(see US Statistical Abstracts, 1995, table 1374, per capita on PPP
basis).

You also need to consider the payroll tax burden:
Payroll tax burden per capita
employer employee total tax burden
US 12.85% 7.65% $6,757
France 31.6 18.27 10,056
Germany 19.8 18.4 11,825
UK 10.4 11.0 6,371
Japan 13.4 11.23 8,694

(see US Statistical Abstracts, 1995, table 1382).

SO, we see that the US worker has a considerably higher tax burden, is
less expensive to employ due to payroll tax, is more productive, and
pays generally lower prices (at least for food).

Another criteria for "standard of living" would be concerned with the
housing we see in the US compared to the EC. A poor family, defined
as below the official poverty line, in the US in 1987 had more room
per person than the average family in the EC in 1980 ("Housing
Charcteristics 1987", US Dept of Energy, Energy Information
Administration, US government Printing Office, 1989). Even more
interesting is a comparison of "Poor" US citizens to the EC countries
in the percentage lacking indoor toilets:

US poor households 1.8%
UK 6
Germany 7 (only West Germany)
Italy 11
Spain 12
France 17
Norway 17
Belgium 19
Ireland 22
Japan 54

So we see an American living below the official poverty line is
several times more likely to have an indoor flush toilet than a
citizen of the EC. Can you imagine not having indoor toilets in
Norway? The data is from 1980, but the proportions are unlikely to
have changed much since the Japanese and EC economies have done very
poorly for the last decade. Data from "Living Conditions in OECD
Countries", Paris OECD, 1986.

Just thought I would mention it.

Regards, Harold

Of course there are many interpretations of what socialism really is.
Many people confuse the concept of socialism with the inevitable
result of it. Socialism basically insists that any means of earning
wealth be owned and operated collectively, albeit with some democratic
process overseeing it. Whereas socialists tell us that it is the
ultimate form of a democracy, it belies the fact that socialism
totally ignores the concept of an individual being able to better
himself, and ultimately denies him individuality itself. It is this
forced slavery to the society, as opposed to the government that most
people oppose. It is the of the simple concept of a man building a
better mousetrap and having taken away from him, that men who cherish
freedom will always oppose socialism.

Some, perhaps most humans will never accept being denied their
individuality, nor the right to reap the rewards of the own work.
Socialism cannot allow this individuality, and will inevitably use
whatever force necessary to force compliance, and of course, this will
lead to a totalitarian government, hence the association of socialism
to totalitarianism.

To better understand the differences between capitalism and socialism,
consider these facts:

Socialism requires special rules and considerations for purposes of
encouraging individual's activity, because the system does not,
capitalism requires them to limit it, because the system abounds in
encouragement.

Capitalism allows individuals to form voluntary socialistic groups
within it, however socialism cannot allow any formation of
capitalistic groups within it's bounds.

Socialism requires a government and police force to enforce it's very
nature, capitalism does not.

Where ever an underground economy exists, it is capitalistic, which is
to say where ever men are free to choose, they chose capitalism.

>
> I knew I had that ratty old thing around here someplace. It
> really sucks. Hmm. I wonder how I'd forgotten that Samuelson was a
> compadre of that Zero-Sum idiot at MIT. In any case, he's been
> trading on the reputation of this book for almost 50 years now. If
> ever there was a case of academic tick syndrome, this is it.

Let's be clear on this. By "Zero-Sum idiot at MIT," one guesses that
Mr. Beck refers to Lester Thurow. Thurow is in the Sloan School of
Management at MIT, Samuelson is in the Department of Economics. Those
are two very different places. Even if they weren't, it is not totally
clear to me why it is important. Perhaps Mr. Beck has some "guilt by
association" theory.

It seems Mr. Beck is onto something, though. Let's take it a little
further. Samuelson was awarded the secondNobel Prize in Economics in
1971. The class of "Nobel Laureates in Economics of the 1970s" is
obviously suspect. I hereby denounce Frederich A. von Hayek and Milton
Friedman for their dastardly association with compadre-idiot Samuelson, and
call upon others to do the same.

It really is remarkable that Samuelson was awarded a Nobel Prize for
writing a textbook. Unless, maybe, he was awarded the prize for
fundamental advances in economic analysis, which gave him a reputation as
one of the great economists of all time, and "traded off" that reputation
by peddling textbooks. It is true that the textbook sales helped to make
Samuelson a rich man. One hopes that this success, in a highly competitive
marketplace (there are a great many textbook authors who would dearly love
to enjoy the success of Samuelson's product) does not elicit the envy of
certain others.

It is true that Samuelson's ratty old thing is full of subversive and
decadent doctrine. For example, Samuelson teaches his readers modern
consumer theory, a body of work to which the author had contributed as
much as anyone. This protosocialist doctrine insists that value is
only and exclusively in the eye of the beholder, that there is neither
need nor validity in comparisons of the utility of several individuals,
and that sovereign consumers will reveal their preferences, which the
careful economist can then passively observe. In another body of work
(which is perhaps not covered in the textbook), our compadre-idiot
considers, then thoroughly demolishes, the idea of a "social welfare
function," which has been used in some analyses of international trade;
Samuelson shows that the attempt to add together individual "utilities"
is doomed from the start, and can lead to nonsensical and even
contradictory results. Instead, Samuelson shows that a useful theory
of international trade must rest within the bounds of consumer theory,
which in turn rests upon a strong notion of individual sovereignty.
Ratty socialistic idiocy, no doubt. Suffering from Lyme Disease, one
suspects, given the prevalence of ticks in the academic forests.


> A word to the wise: read this book, and then move on.

Assuming the alternative courses of action are

(a) read this book, and then move on,
(b) read this book, then stop,
(c) skip the book, then move on,
and
(d) stop,

I endorse Mr. Beck's word to the wise. Except for Mr. Sam, of course, who
doesn't read books.

I'll start with three side items that came up earlier in the thread.

First, it is true that Samuelson was the first American Nobel Laureate
in economics. He was, in fact, only the second Nobel laureate in
economics at all. The prize was not funded by the Nobel bequest, rather
was tacked on later, by the Norwegians. If memory serves, which is rare
enough, the year before Samuelson won, the first prize went to Jan
Tinbergen, who I *think* is Norwegian.

Second, Laura Tyson's name was invoked (I believe by Mr. Starr) as an
extension of the tactic of smear-by-association (in the curious belief
that association with the MIT Department of Economics could somehow be
turned into a smear). As proof that Tyson is a fool and a scoundrel, it
was proposed that she had stated that the Rumanian dictatorship of the
1970s and 1980s provided a laudable model of economic organization. I
suspect that this proposition is spurious; I have seen it before, but
never with either a cite or context, and it does not square with what I
have heard from Tyson. Tyson's graduate-school specialty was
"comparative systems," which involves modelling of key features of economic
systems in different countries. Her greatest interest in that study was
the Territories Formerly Known as Yugoslavia; she built a model of the
worker-managed enterprise (which was the hallmark of "Yugoslavian
Communism"). Her thesis: the system had the decentralization of
decisionmaking characteristic of capitalism, and therefore offered a
solution to the calculation problem which (as Hayek demonstrated)
afflicts any centrally-planned economy, on the other hand if workers
paid themselves their marginal value product, and capital nothing (since
in the Yugoslavian system the state rationed capital), they would try to
overequip, and the growth rate of the economy would be slower than the
benchmark. The benchmark, of course, was the standard free capitalist
economy. It would not be surprising if Tyson studied some of the
economies around Yugoslavia; I don't recall those specifics (since these
are memories of an undergraduate classroom, with new-professor Tyson at
the rostrum, almost 20 years ago). I do recall that she was generally
very unfavorable to the centrally-planned economies, and to the extent
that she offered *Yugoslavia* as a model to emulate, it was precisely to
those centrally-planned economies. Now perhaps in her old age, and
after Tyson got more involved in work on the economies of Western
Europe, she changed her mind, and decided that Romania was some sort of
a Paradise. For that matter, she may have decided that Envher Hoxha was
the man to lead us into the Red Dawn of a New Socialist Day. I doubt
it, but I could be convinced otherwise. With evidence.

Against the sin of having been an a department in which Laura
Tyson once studied, Mr. Starr offers as a palliative the name of Paul
Krugman. Whereas I doubt that Tyson spent very much time with
Samuelson, unless he was teaching one of the core courses, since
Samuelson has done no work in comparative systems, the opposite is
likely true of Krugman. Krugman's specialties are international trade
and growth, areas of general-equilibrium theory whose modern
Foundations were laid by Samuelson (Samuelson's doctoral dissertation
was published under the title of *Foundations of Economic Analysis*; it
is not mistitled). In fact, Tyson's work, which is generally
descriptive, and tied to people and places, is rather anachronistic,
especially at MIT, which is one of the homes (following Samuelson!) of
fairly abstract mathematical economics.

And so to the main course.

> "Political economy was, in effect, a science starting in
> midstream: it observed that men were producing and trading, it took
> for granted that they had always done so and always would - it
> accepted this idea as the given, requiring no futher consideration -
> and it addressed itself to the problem of how to devise the best way
> to for the 'community' to dispose of human effort."
>
> (Ayn Rand - "What Is Capitalism", 1965)

Some of this sounds right, and other parts mis-aimed---I suspect because
of changes in the discipline. If it is applied to the classical
political economists---say through John Stuart Mills, and perhaps one
wants to stick Marx in there---I think it is bang-on, if a rather
scholastic proposition in the history of economic thought. If it is
applied to the moderns, which I want to start with Samuelson (although
with links to Marshall) and the Cambridge neo-classicists, I think it is
only half right, and even less relevant, "it observed that men were
producing and trading...and always would."

The core of modern economics is the so-called positive program,
on which Friedman has written eloquently. The objective of that
program, which is distinguished from the "normative" program, is simply
to understand, and to test that understanding by prediction. To the
extent that there are formal links to philosophy, is to epistemology
rather than to ethics, I guess. At this point, I stray out of my
depth, and anticipate correction. Samuelson's model was mathematical
physics, a discipline that is more concerned with laws of motion,
instantaneous rates of change, and with equilibrium states, studied
through the device of comparative statics, than it is with untestable
propositions. This is at the root of Samuelson's use of the axioms
of consumer theory. Assuming that the utilities of two individuals can
be measured, compared, and combined yields no hypotheses that can be
tested, beyond what can be done with the weakest axioms. The modelling
strategy is driven by logic and epistemology. The suggestion that one should
take into account ethics, in a research program that is concerned
above all with understanding what *is*, is indeed, as you say, "curious."

I deny the second part of Rand's statement, at least as a statement of the
core of modern economics. Yes, economists will make predictions about
how individuals' choice will vary given specified changes in the
circumstances that they face (such as taxes or subsidies, or state
provision of goods); furthermore, economists can make predictions about
how aggregates behave. And yes, economists can and do make statements
about Pareto improvement, which is about as close to ethics as we dare
get: given an allocation, a set of rules, and a change in something,
will peoples' opportunity set be enlarged? Can some people alter their
choices to improve their own utility, by their own lights, leaving no
other person worse off than they were before?

Some of us do dare to venture into the perilous waters of Political
Economy. But again, in the modern sense, our program is positive:
"what causes political institutions to be as they are?" Yes, sometimes
we want to tweak the institutions. In most cases, this involves trying
to get the prices and marketplaces back into operation, to let people
trade off their preferences openly, and to shut down the distorting
filter of vested interest and congressman.

See, this is the way to keep people from taking you seriously.
Socialism is a broad term, used for everything from European welfare
states to Mao's China, and also including any number of voluntary forms--
communes, collectives and so forth. Communism is more narrowly defined,
and usually means socialism with no (or very few) capitalist elements
mixed in. The Bolsheviks were a particular party of communists, who
eventually gained control of the Soviet Union. The three words have
distinct definitions, and when you conflate them for propaganda purposes,
your avoiding thought and robbing the language.
